weeks.title: Polynomial structure and identities
weeks.objective: Combine, expand, and factor polynomials while explaining degree and equivalent forms.
days: Sort expressions by whether they are polynomials; combine signed coefficients in worksheet A.
Distribute every term in the first worked example and compare expanded and factored forms.
Derive square and difference-of-squares identities; use worksheet B to repair omitted mixed terms.
Model courtyard area and box volume with worksheet C; attach squared and cubed units.
Prove the difference-of-squares comparison and explain how leading-term cancellation changes degree.
explanation: A polynomial in x is a finite sum of terms ax^n with nonnegative integer exponents n. Its degree is the greatest exponent with a nonzero coefficient after like terms are combined. The coefficient belongs to the entire term: subtracting a polynomial changes every sign inside its parentheses. A table of degrees and coefficients can keep missing powers visible.

Multiplication uses the distributive law for every pair of terms. The leading terms predict the degree of a nonzero product, while cancellation can lower the degree of a sum. Identities are equations true for every permitted input. For instance, (u+v)(u−v)=u^2−v^2 because the two mixed products cancel; it is not a rule for u^2+v^2 over the reals.

Factored and expanded forms describe the same polynomial but expose different information. Factors can reveal zeros, and expanded terms can reveal degree or combine models. Verify a factorization by multiplying; a single matching numerical value is only a check, not a proof of identity. Treat dimensions separately: a length times a length gives area, not another length.

weeks.title: Factors, zeros, and graph behavior
weeks.objective: Connect real factors, multiplicity, signs, and end behavior.
days: Recover zeros from factors and distinguish distinct roots from multiplicity using worksheet A.
Sketch crossing and touching behavior near each zero in the first worked example.
Build interval sign charts and least-degree polynomials in worksheet B.
Use an additional point to determine the scale factor; impose positive box dimensions in worksheet C.
Compare zero locations, multiplicities, end behavior, and feasible intervals in one labeled sketch.
explanation: A zero is an input where the polynomial output is zero. The zero-product property lets a product vanish when at least one factor vanishes. A factor x−r gives the zero r; a factor x+r gives −r. Repeated copies of the same factor give multiplicity. This counts algebraic repetition rather than distinct intercept locations.

Near a zero r, all other nonzero factors keep their sign. The factor (x−r)^m changes sign across r when m is odd and keeps its sign when m is even. Thus an odd-multiplicity zero crosses the horizontal axis; an even-multiplicity zero touches and turns back locally. A sign chart needs test points in the intervals separated by the zeros, not just values at the zeros themselves.

For large positive or negative inputs, the leading term determines end behavior. Even degree gives matching ends; odd degree gives opposite ends, with the leading coefficient deciding direction. A factored model with prescribed zeros still needs a scale factor. One additional nonzero point can determine that factor, and substitution then checks the constructed rule.

weeks.title: Polynomial division and remainders
weeks.objective: Divide polynomials and connect the remainder to evaluation and factors.

connection.before: Factored forms and evaluation at zeros.

days: Connect the zero of a linear divisor to evaluation in worksheet A.

Explain why a nonzero remainder rules out a factor; reconstruct one dividend from quotient and remainder.
explanation: Polynomial division rewrites P(x) as D(x)Q(x)+R(x), where the remainder has smaller degree than the divisor. Divide leading terms, multiply the entire divisor by the next quotient term, then subtract and repeat. Include a zero coefficient for each missing power so unlike terms never slide into the same column.

For a linear divisor x−r, the remainder is constant. Substitute x=r in P(x)=(x−r)Q(x)+R: the product disappears, leaving P(r)=R. This proves the Remainder Theorem. It also proves the Factor Theorem: x−r is a factor exactly when P(r)=0. A divisor x+4 corresponds to r=−4, not 4.

Division can reveal a useful factor, but a quotient alone is not the original polynomial. Reconstruct the dividend by divisor times quotient plus remainder. If the division is written as a fraction, the expression Q(x)+R(x)/D(x) keeps the original restriction D(x)≠0. That restriction will be central in the next unit.

weeks.title: Complex numbers and arithmetic
weeks.objective: Use i^2=−1 to add, subtract, and multiply complex numbers.
days: Define i^2=−1 and organize real and imaginary parts while completing worksheet A.

Build the four-power cycle of i and use it to explain the large-exponent calculations.
explanation: The real numbers do not contain a number whose square is −1. Define i by i^2=−1, and write a complex number as a+bi, where a and b are real. Equality requires equal real parts and equal imaginary coefficients. A negative real radicand can be represented by √(−c)=i√c for c>0 when the principal square root is intended.

Add or subtract real parts together and imaginary coefficients together. Multiplication still uses distribution, followed by replacing every i^2 with −1. Powers cycle: i, −1, −i, 1, then repeat. This lets a large power reduce to its exponent remainder on division by 4. The imaginary unit is a number, not a variable whose square can be left unspecified.

The real-number rule √u√v=√(uv) cannot be applied indiscriminately to negative radicands using principal complex roots. For example √(−1)√(−1)=i^2=−1, while √1=1. A product of conjugate forms (a+bi)(a−bi) is real because mixed terms cancel and −b^2i^2 becomes +b^2. Check a result by expanding or reversing an addition.

weeks.title: Quadratics with complex solutions
weeks.objective: Solve real-coefficient quadratics and verify nonreal roots.

connection.before: Complex multiplication and completing the square.

days: Classify discriminants and distinguish complex roots from real graph intercepts in worksheet A.

explanation: Completing the square remains useful when the square would need to equal a negative number. From (x−h)^2=−k, k>0, the two solutions are h+i√k and h−i√k. The ± symbol records two roots. The principal radical alone is one value; an equation asking which numbers square to the radicand usually has two.

For ax^2+bx+c=0 with a≠0, the discriminant b^2−4ac tells whether the quadratic formula gives two distinct real roots, one repeated real root, or two nonreal conjugate roots. A negative discriminant does not mean the equation has no complex solutions. A real-coordinate graph has no x-intercepts in that case, because its horizontal inputs are real.

Check a nonreal root by substitution using i^2=−1. For real coefficients the conjugate partner appears too; their sum and product are real. A quadratic can be factored over the complex numbers even when it has no real linear factors. Keep this algebraic fact separate from any context that only permits real, nonnegative measurements.

weeks.title: Polynomial symmetry and synthesis
weeks.objective: Classify even/odd functions and compare polynomial representations.

connection.before: Polynomial roots, complex solutions, and transformations.

days: Check symmetric domains before classifying even, odd, both, or neither in worksheet A.
Substitute −x into both example functions and connect the identities to graph symmetry.
Translate between vertex, expanded, and factored forms with worksheet B.
Find coefficient conditions for even or odd polynomials in worksheet C.
Defend a symmetry classification algebraically and explain why matching two data points is insufficient.
explanation: An even function has f(−x)=f(x) on a domain symmetric about zero; its graph reflects across the vertical axis. An odd function has f(−x)=−f(x); its graph has half-turn symmetry around the origin. Check the domain first, then substitute the opposite input into the entire rule. A function can be neither, and the zero function satisfies both identities.

Polynomials with only even powers and a constant are even; polynomials with only odd powers and no nonzero constant are odd. These claims follow by substituting −x into each power. Horizontal or vertical translations can destroy origin-based symmetry. A parabola shifted sideways may still have a symmetry line, but that line is not necessarily the vertical axis required by the definition of even.

Use a form that matches the question. Factored form displays real zeros, vertex form displays quadratic turning behavior, and expanded form displays degree and coefficients. Compare functions through common inputs, domains, and features, not appearances alone. A few symmetric data pairs can refute a proposed identity when they fail, but cannot prove it for every real input.

examples.prompt: Classify f(x)=x^4−3x^2+2 and g(x)=x^3+x+1.
examples.answer: f is even; g is neither
steps: f(−x)=x^4−3x^2+2=f(x), and its domain is all real numbers.
g(−x)=−x^3−x+1, which differs from g(x) and from −g(x)=−x^3−x−1.
For a concrete failure, g(1)=3 and g(−1)=−1; these are neither equal nor opposites.

examples.prompt: Compare p(x)=(x−2)^2−1 and q(x)=x^2−4x+3.
examples.answer: They are identical; vertex (2,−1), zeros 1 and 3; neither even nor odd
steps: Expand p to x^2−4x+4−1=q.
Factor q as (x−1)(x−3) to obtain the zeros.
The vertex lies on x=2; p(1)=0 but p(−1)=8, ruling out both parity identities.

weeks.title: Rational exponents and irrational structure
weeks.objective: Interpret rational powers and distinguish justified rational/irrational conclusions.

connection.before: Integer exponent laws and real square roots.

days: Translate rational exponents into roots and powers; complete worksheet A with sign checks.

Give examples and contradiction arguments separating rational and irrational sums and products.
explanation: For a positive base a, a^(m/n) means the nth root of a raised to the integer power m, with n positive. This definition preserves exponent laws: raising a^(1/n) to the nth power gives a. Reduce rational exponents before interpreting a negative real base; odd roots allow negative radicands, while even roots do not give real values for them.

A principal square root is nonnegative. Thus √(x^2)=|x|, not x for every real input. Simplifying radicals extracts perfect-power factors while retaining any variable restrictions. Negative exponents mean reciprocals and require nonzero bases. Parentheses distinguish (−8)^(1/3), which is −2, from a minus sign outside an unrelated power.

Rational numbers are closed under addition and multiplication. A rational number plus an irrational number is irrational: otherwise subtraction would make the irrational number rational. The product of a nonzero rational and an irrational is also irrational, but products of two irrational numbers can be rational or irrational. Give examples or a contradiction argument instead of deciding from decimal appearance.

weeks.objective: Construct square-root and cube-root graphs from complete tables and restrictions.

explanation: The graph y=√x begins at (0,0), has domain x≥0 and range y≥0, and continues to the right. Choose inputs that make perfect squares to obtain exact points. In y=a√(x−h)+k, the endpoint is (h,k). The sign of a determines upward or downward reflection, and its magnitude scales vertical distances from k.

The real cube-root function continues in both directions: its domain and range are all real numbers. It passes through (−8,−2),(0,0),(8,2), and its graph has origin symmetry. A translated cube-root graph has a center of symmetry but no endpoint. Label that distinction explicitly rather than extending a square-root sketch into forbidden inputs.

Average rate of change on [u,v] is (f(v)−f(u))/(v−u), with both endpoints in the domain. It describes a secant slope, not a constant rate for the whole curve. Transformations act on inputs and outputs differently: x−h moves a graph right h, while adding k moves it up. Check a predicted transformed point by substitution.

weeks.objective: Rewrite polynomial quotients without losing excluded inputs.
days: Factor denominators and list every excluded input before simplifying worksheet A.

Explain why cancellation cannot restore a forbidden input; verify a rewritten expression at legal values.
explanation: A rational expression is a quotient of polynomials. Begin by identifying all real zeros of the original denominator: none are allowed inputs. Factoring may expose a common factor, but cancellation is division by that factor and is valid only where the factor is nonzero. Write the restriction beside the simplified expression so the original function is preserved.

Use polynomial division when the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree. The identity P=DQ+R gives P/D=Q+R/D on the domain D≠0. This is an equivalent expression there, including when the remainder is zero. It does not grant permission to restore a previously excluded input.

Cancellation applies to factors of an entire product, not to selected terms of sums. For example (x+2)/x is 1+2/x, not 2. Test an alleged equivalence with a legal input to detect a failure, and use factorization or reconstruction to establish an identity. This week concerns expressions and domains, leaving full rational-graph analysis to the optional advanced pathway.

explanation: An equation containing rational expressions asks which permitted inputs make two values equal. State denominator restrictions before multiplying. Multiplication by a common denominator preserves equivalence only where it is nonzero; a resulting polynomial equation may include a forbidden candidate. Solve that equation, then test every candidate in the original statement.

Choose a least common denominator or another common multiple and multiply every term on both sides. Missing a constant term is a common error. For 1/x+2=5/x, multiplication by x gives 1+2x=5, not 1+2=5. A solution check evaluates both original sides numerically or exactly, rather than merely repeating the cleared equation.

In a rate model, keep quantities and units visible. If a fixed job is one whole, a completion time t gives a rate 1/t jobs per hour; rates add for simultaneous independent work at constant pace. Positive time restrictions may reject algebraically permitted negative answers. The context can narrow the domain beyond denominator exclusions.

weeks.title: Radical equations and extraneous roots
weeks.objective: Use sign conditions and original-equation checks after squaring.

connection.before: Real root domains and equation transformations.

days: Identify nonnegative-radicand and nonnegative-output conditions before worksheet A.
Work both examples and explain why squaring may add candidates.
Solve worksheet B by isolating radicals and checking each candidate in the original equation.
Use worksheet C to select valid radical roots and positive geometric lengths.
Contrast squaring with cubing and write a complete explanation of one extraneous solution.
explanation: A square-root equation has two immediate constraints: its radicand must be nonnegative, and its principal root is nonnegative. If √A(x)=B(x), any solution must satisfy both A(x)≥0 and B(x)≥0. Squaring gives A(x)=B(x)^2, but that equation alone cannot distinguish B from −B.

Isolate a radical before squaring. Solve the resulting equation and substitute each candidate into the original, unsquared equation. A candidate that fails is called extraneous: it solved a transformed equation but not the original. Squaring both sides is a useful implication, not automatically a reversible equivalence.

Odd powers behave differently over the real numbers: cubing is one-to-one and a real cube root can be negative. Equations with one cube root often reverse directly without sign loss. For geometric applications, check both algebraic restrictions and measurement conditions. A squared length equation can admit a negative number that has no physical meaning.

examples.prompt: Solve √(x+6)=x.
steps: The right side must be nonnegative, so x≥0.
Square: x+6=x^2, hence (x−3)(x+2)=0.
The candidate −2 fails the sign condition; at 3, √9=3 verifies the sole solution.
Isolate √(2x+3)=3, whose right side is nonnegative.
Square to get 2x+3=9, so x=3.
The original equation gives √9+1=4; the radicand is allowed.

weeks.title: Simple inverses and reversible models
weeks.objective: Solve for inverse rules and exchange domains and ranges.
days: Reverse input-output pairs in tables and identify repeated outputs using worksheet A.
Solve the linear inverse example by reversing operations in reverse order.
Restrict a quadratic domain and explain why one square-root branch is selected.
Use worksheet B and the rental/sensor tasks to exchange domains and ranges precisely.
Compare an inverse with a reciprocal and verify a forward-backward pair from worksheet C.
explanation: An inverse reverses a function’s input-output assignment. To find a simple inverse, name the output y, solve the equation for x, and then express the reverse rule with a new input variable. The inverse is not the reciprocal 1/f(x). A one-to-one rule assigns different outputs to different inputs; otherwise reversing would send one input to multiple outputs.

The original domain becomes the inverse range, and the original range becomes the inverse domain. A quadratic on all real inputs is not one-to-one because opposite offsets from its vertex match. Restricting to one side of the vertex can make the reversal a function. A square-root inverse carries a domain inherited from nonnegative outputs, rather than accepting every algebraically convenient input.

A conversion model makes the reversal concrete: if cost is fixed fee plus a rate times quantity, subtract the fixed fee before dividing by the rate. Reverse the operations in reverse order. Check a pair of values forward and backward with units; tables also show whether a repeated output would prevent a unique inverse.

examples.prompt: Find the inverse of f(x)=4x−7 on R.
steps: Write y=4x−7 and add 7 to get y+7=4x.
Divide by 4 to solve x=(y+7)/4, then name the inverse input x.
For original input 3 the output is 5, and the reverse rule sends 5 to 3.

examples.prompt: Find the inverse of f(x)=(x−1)^2 for x≥1.
steps: The original outputs are nonnegative and x−1≥0.
From y=(x−1)^2 take the nonnegative root: √y=x−1.
Thus x=1+√y; the inverse accepts y≥0 and returns x≥1.

weeks.title: Exponential growth and decay
weeks.objective: Build multiplicative models with explicit time units and domains.
days: Translate percentage change into per-step multipliers using worksheet A.
Build the two worked models with explicit day and hour units.
Recover a positive exponential base from separated data points in worksheet B.
Compare discrete counts, depreciation, and capacity constraints in worksheet C.
Explain the difference between constant ratios and constant differences and test a long-term extrapolation.
explanation: In f(t)=Ab^t, A is the output at t=0 and b>0 is the factor for one input unit. A percentage increase r uses b=1+r, while a decrease r uses b=1−r. A 15% loss leaves 85%, so its factor is 0.85, not 0.15. State what one unit of t means before interpreting the rate.

Equal input steps produce equal output ratios in a pure exponential model, whereas a linear model produces equal differences. Two positive outputs at times separated by h units determine b^h as their ratio. A factor quoted every three hours must be converted to an hourly factor by a cube root if the model uses hours.

A discrete process may be defined only at whole-number steps even when its formula can be evaluated between them. A continuous extension is an assumption requiring context. Growth models often stop being plausible far beyond observed times because resources or capacity change. Keep exact powers during work and round measured outputs only at the requested stage.

examples.prompt: A culture model starts at 500 units and grows by 20% each day. Write N(t) and find N(3).
steps: The initial value at day zero is 500.
A 20% increase multiplies by 1.20 each day.
Three repeated multiplications give 500·1.728=864; use whole days unless a continuous model is assumed.

examples.prompt: A mass halves every 4 hours, starting at 80 g. Model t hours and find the mass at 12 hours.
steps: The number of half-life intervals is t/4.
Raise the half-factor to that number of intervals.
At 12 hours there are 3 halvings, giving 80/8=10 g.

weeks.title: Logarithms as unknown exponents
weeks.objective: Translate logarithmic statements and solve exponential equations.
days: Translate between logarithmic and exponential statements and establish positive-argument domains.
Solve the first model exactly with logarithms, then check its rounded value by exponentiation.
Build logarithm graph points and shifted zeros with worksheet B.
Solve continuous-time and whole-day threshold questions in worksheet C.
Explain why base 1 and nonpositive arguments fail and distinguish a real threshold from its first integer crossing.
explanation: For b>0 and b≠1, log_b(y) is the exponent that makes b^x=y, and it requires y>0. The statement log_2(8)=3 means 2^3=8. A logarithm is an exponent value, not multiplication by a mysterious symbol. Negative logarithm outputs are allowed: they represent positive values below 1 when the base exceeds 1.

To solve Ab^(kt)=C with A,C positive, first isolate b^(kt)=C/A. Taking natural logarithms gives kt·ln(b)=ln(C/A), so t=ln(C/A)/(k ln b), provided k≠0. Here ln is the logarithm with base e, where e≈2.71828; a calculator evaluates it. Keep the exact quotient until final rounding. Substitute the approximation into the original exponential to judge its accuracy.

The graph y=log_b x reverses the input-output pairs of y=b^x: it passes through (1,0) and has domain x>0. For b>1 it increases, with very negative outputs as x approaches zero from the right. Logarithmic models cannot accept zero or negative arguments. A shift such as log_2(x−3) requires x>3 and moves the zero to x=4.

examples.prompt: Solve 3·2^t=21 exactly and approximately to two decimals.
steps: Divide by 3 to isolate 2^t=7.
Take logarithms: t ln2=ln7.
Divide by ln2; the result lies between 2 and 3 because 4<7<8.

Solve x+2=1; substituting −1 gives log_3(1)=0.

ln3 is about 1.10, so it cannot be the same value.

weeks.title: Comparing exponential and logarithmic change
weeks.objective: Interpret transformed functions and distinguish absolute from proportional rates.
days: Compare percentage growth with absolute change and compute the worksheet A secant slopes.
Separate baseline and changing excess in the first worked model.
Use worksheet B tables to analyze transformations and shifted exponential ranges.
Compare linear growth with compounding and interpret cooling in worksheet C.
Explain why constant proportional change does not give constant average slope or justify indefinite growth.
explanation: An exponential may change by the same percentage each interval while its absolute increments grow or shrink. Compute both differences and ratios before choosing a model. Average rate of change is an absolute change per input unit; it is not the exponential percentage rate. Units prevent confusing these two descriptions.

Adding a constant creates a baseline: f(t)=K+Ab^t. The total outputs generally no longer have constant ratios, but their differences from K do. A negative exponent reverses growth direction, and replacing t by t−h delays a pattern by h units. State the context domain even if the algebraic expression accepts a wider set.

Logarithmic change reverses exponential change. Equal multipliers in the input of log_b x produce equal additions to its output. Compare different function families using supplied tables and contextual limits: rapid long-term exponential growth can eventually exceed a linear or polynomial rule, but a few early values do not identify the crossing or justify unlimited real-world growth.

As the positive decaying part approaches zero, outputs approach 10 from above.

explanation: A sequence is a function whose inputs are an ordered set of integers, commonly n=1,2,3,… . State where indexing begins. The nth term is one output, while a sum of the first n terms is a different quantity. An arithmetic sequence adds a fixed difference; a geometric sequence multiplies by a fixed ratio.

If the first term is a1, an arithmetic rule is a_n=a1+(n−1)d and a geometric rule is a_n=a1 r^(n−1). The exponent n−1 counts transitions after the first term. Recursive rules specify the initial term and how to obtain the next, such as a_n=r a_(n−1) for n≥2. Without an initial value a recurrence does not identify one sequence.

A recursive model may mix a multiplier and a new addition, as when an amount grows and then receives a contribution. Such a recurrence is usually neither arithmetic nor geometric. Check operation order: adding before growth differs from adding afterward. Use a short table to verify any proposed explicit rule and label whether a term counts a beginning or ending balance.

weeks.title: Finite geometric sums
weeks.objective: Derive and use finite series without confusing terms and totals.
days: List terms before using a sum formula; distinguish the final term from the total in worksheet A.

Use worksheet B for negative ratios, decreasing positive terms, and off-by-one errors.

Check totals by direct addition and explain the separate r=1 case.
explanation: A finite geometric sum adds a fixed number of successive terms a,ar,ar^2,…,ar^(n−1). Multiplying the sum S by r shifts every term one position. Subtract rS from S and all interior terms cancel, leaving (1−r)S=a−ar^n. Thus S=a(1−r^n)/(1−r) for r≠1; when r=1 simply add a n times.

The exponent in the last term is n−1, but the closed sum contains r^n because the shifted copy has one extra power. This difference causes frequent off-by-one errors. Write a short list of terms before substituting. Ratios less than one produce decreasing terms, yet their cumulative totals still rise when terms are positive.

An accumulating-payment model must state when each contribution enters. For example three deposits made at the ends of three periods earn respectively two, one, and zero growth intervals by the end of the third period. Their future values form a finite geometric sum in reverse order. State the modeled rate and exclude fees or other changes only when the scenario expressly assumes them absent.

weeks.objective: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide functions with correct interpretation and domains.
days: Match addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division to model quantities and units.

Defend one combined rule with units, feasible inputs, and a check against its component quantities.
explanation: Combining functions by arithmetic preserves the meaning of the operation only when the quantities fit. Revenue minus cost gives profit, while price times quantity gives revenue. Adding lengths to dollars has no coherent unit. The domain of a combined model must satisfy every component and any new denominator restriction.

A baseline plus a decaying excess, T(t)=A+Bq^t, separates a stable background from a changing contribution. Revenue R(n)=np(n) may be quadratic even when the price p(n) is linear. Average cost C(n)/n requires n>0 for a positive production context. These are arithmetic combinations: composition would feed one function’s output into another as its input.

After building a rule, explain its coefficients and check a specific input against the original quantities. A mathematically defined output can be economically or physically impossible, such as a negative price or fractional count. State integer requirements, valid intervals, and rounding conventions; a prediction beyond the observed or feasible domain needs new justification.

weeks.title: Radians and circular motion
weeks.objective: Connect radian measure, arc length, and unit-circle coordinates.

connection.before: Geometry arc length and right-triangle ratios.
connection.after: Sine and cosine at angles beyond one quadrant.

days: Convert degrees and radians and calculate arc lengths with matched length units.
Track counterclockwise quarter-turns in the unit-circle example.
Use worksheet B to compare signed angles, coterminal angles, and scaled coordinates.

Explain why a full turn preserves sine and cosine while increasing accumulated radian measure.
explanation: An angle’s radian measure is arc length divided by radius: θ=s/r. Both lengths must use the same units, making the radian a ratio. A full circumference is 2πr, so a complete revolution is 2π radians. Angles in this unit are not degrees: π radians corresponds to 180 degrees.

On a circle centered at the origin, begin at the positive horizontal axis. Positive angles rotate counterclockwise; negative angles rotate clockwise. A unit circle has radius 1, so the radian angle equals its signed arc length numerically. After any whole number of turns the terminal point repeats, although the accumulated angle may differ.

The coordinates of the unit-circle point are (cosθ,sinθ). On a radius-r circle they become (r cosθ,r sinθ). This definition extends right-triangle ratios beyond acute angles and lets signs come from position: left means negative cosine, below means negative sine. Keep angle units explicit, particularly when using a calculator.

weeks.title: Sine and cosine around the unit circle
weeks.objective: Determine exact values, signs, and periodic coordinates.
days: Read sine and cosine as vertical and horizontal coordinates at the four axis points.
Use a reference triangle and quadrant signs to work the 5π/6 example.
Complete worksheet B with coterminal angles and all solutions in specified intervals.
Use worksheet C to convert unit-circle values into scaled heights and coordinates.
Explain why reference-angle magnitudes need quadrant signs and why interval endpoints affect solution lists.
explanation: Sine is the unit-circle vertical coordinate, and cosine is the horizontal coordinate. The four axis points give values at 0,π/2,π,3π/2 immediately. For other angles, familiar 30–60–90 and 45–45–90 triangles determine coordinate magnitudes. The quadrant supplies the signs, so a reference triangle alone is not the full answer.

The point at π/6 has coordinates (√3/2,1/2), and the point at π/4 has coordinates (√2/2,√2/2). Reflecting a point across an axis changes one coordinate’s sign while retaining both magnitudes. Use this geometric reflection to locate obtuse, negative, or larger-than-one-turn angles. Reduce by whole turns when helpful.

Both functions have domain all real radian inputs and range [−1,1]. Their graphs repeat every 2π, but at a given angle the two coordinates need not be equal. A zero of sine lies on the horizontal axis; a zero of cosine lies on the vertical axis. When asked for solutions, give every angle in the stated interval and check whether the right endpoint is included.

weeks.objective: Derive sin^2θ+cos^2θ=1 and use quadrant information.
days: Derive the Pythagorean identity from the unit-circle distance equation.

explanation: A point (x,y) on the unit circle satisfies x^2+y^2=1 by the distance formula. Substituting x=cosθ and y=sinθ gives cos^2θ+sin^2θ=1 for every real angle. The notation sin^2θ means (sinθ)^2, not sin(θ^2); parentheses can make this distinction clear.

If one coordinate is known, subtract its square from 1 to find the other coordinate’s square. Taking a square root gives two possible signs unless the quadrant or another condition selects one. For instance sinθ=3/5 alone allows cosθ=±4/5; specifying quadrant II selects −4/5. An angle on an axis should be handled directly rather than assigned to a quadrant interior.

Identity-based simplification is valid throughout the common domain of both expressions. Dividing by sinθ or cosθ adds a nonzero restriction, even if a later simplification no longer displays the denominator. Check a proposed identity symbolically or refute it with one explicit angle. A numerical match at one angle cannot prove equality for all angles.

explanation: In y=D+A sin(Bt) or y=D+A cos(Bt) with B>0, the midline is D, amplitude is |A|, and period is 2π/B. The range is [D−|A|,D+|A|]. Amplitude is half the peak-to-trough distance, not the largest output unless the midline is zero.

A full cycle can be sketched from five quarter-period points. A positive cosine starts at a maximum; a positive sine starts on the midline moving upward. Multiplying by a negative reflects the pattern across the midline. Horizontal shift changes where the cycle starts but not its amplitude or length.

A context domain may include only part of the indefinitely repeating graph. Label time and output units, and choose radians when evaluating a model containing π. The parameter B measures radians per time unit, so it is not the period itself. Verify a proposed period by showing the angle advances exactly 2π after that many time units.

explanation: To fit a sinusoid, first identify an appropriate repeating phenomenon and a consistent time unit. Estimate the midline by averaging maximum and minimum, the amplitude by halving their difference, and the period from consecutive matching cycle positions. Two peaks are consecutive only if the data or context says no peak lies between.

Choose a phase using a known starting position. A maximum at time h fits D+A cos(B(t−h)) with A>0. A minimum fits D−A cos(B(t−h)), and an upward midline crossing fits positive sine. Different-looking formulas may describe the same cycle; verify agreement at key positions rather than declaring one expression uniquely correct.

Exact invented cycle data can fit an ideal sinusoid perfectly, but measured or noisy data need a tolerance and a stated approximation. A few sampled values can hide extra cycles between observations. Predictions should acknowledge the assumed period, constant amplitude, and relevant time range. Check all supplied quarter-cycle points when available.

explanation: A periodic target can be reached more than once per cycle. First isolate sine or cosine and check whether the required value lies in [−1,1]. Use unit-circle positions for familiar values, convert the resulting angles to times, and retain all times in the stated interval. The interval endpoints may represent the same position at distinct times.

Average change over a full period is zero because the initial and final heights agree. This does not imply no motion; the object may travel a substantial distance while returning to its starting height. Shorter-interval secant slopes may be positive, zero, or negative. State whether the question asks displacement, total travel, or average rate.

Compare cycles through separate features: equal amplitude does not imply equal period or phase. In real applications a smooth sinusoid may only approximate noisy observations, and a target can be physically impossible despite a formal equation. weeks.objective: Separate random sampling, random assignment, and observational association.
days: Identify populations, samples, sampling frames, and observed variables in worksheet A.
Contrast random selection with random treatment assignment using the two worked studies.
Identify confounding, nonresponse, and allocation problems in worksheet B.
Use worksheet C to separate causal scope from population generalization in mixed-stage designs.
Revise an overbroad study conclusion by preserving the observed association and naming its specific limits.
explanation: A population is the collection a study aims to describe; a sample is the subset observed. Random selection from a population helps make sampling-based generalization defensible when the sampling frame and response are adequate. A large convenience sample can still be biased because size alone does not correct which people were available or chose to respond.

Random assignment is a different operation: it allocates recruited subjects to treatment conditions. A well-conducted randomized experiment can support a causal comparison for its study conditions because assignment reduces systematic confounding. Random selection without treatment assignment does not turn an association into causation. Assignment among volunteers does not by itself justify generalizing to everyone.

Observational studies record existing behaviors or exposures. A lurking variable may influence both the explanatory variable and response, so competing explanations remain. Describe what was measured, how subjects entered, and whether a treatment was assigned before judging the conclusion. Ethical or practical constraints may favor observation, but do not erase its causal limitations.

examples.prompt: A school randomly selects 80 students, records sleep hours and quiz scores, and finds a positive association. What can the design support?
examples.answer: An association estimate for the school’s students, subject to sampling/response limits; not a causal sleep effect
steps: Selection is random from the named school population.
Sleep is observed rather than randomly assigned.
Other factors may influence both sleep and scores, so the association cannot by itself establish causation.

examples.prompt: Forty volunteers are randomly assigned to two practice formats. One group has a larger mean improvement. State a warranted scope.
examples.answer: A treatment comparison among these volunteers under the study conditions; broad population generalization is not assured

Volunteer recruitment is not random selection from a wider population.
Use the randomized comparison for causal evidence while limiting external generalization.

weeks.title: Normal models and standardized distances
weeks.objective: Use supplied normal probabilities with mean and standard deviation.

connection.before: Quantitative distributions and measures of center/spread.

days: Standardize measurements and reverse z-scores with explicit mean and positive standard deviation.
Use symmetry to apply the 68–95–99.7 rule in the first example.
Subtract supplied cumulative probabilities to find intervals and tails in worksheet B.
Use worksheet C to connect normal percentages to expected counts and question inappropriate shapes.
Distinguish individual spread from an exact sample-count claim and explain why a point has zero continuous-model probability.
explanation: A normal model is a symmetric bell-shaped probability distribution specified by mean μ and positive standard deviation σ. Standardizing x as z=(x−μ)/σ measures how many standard deviations x lies above or below the mean. A negative z is below the mean; changing the unit of measurement changes μ and σ together, leaving z unchanged.

For an appropriate normal model, approximately 68% lies within one standard deviation, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three. Symmetry splits leftover tails equally. These are model approximations, not facts about every dataset. For more precise calculations use supplied cumulative values Φ(z)=P(Z≤z); an interval probability is the upper cumulative value minus the lower.

Check shape and context before imposing normality. Strong skew, severe outliers, or a distribution with separate clusters may make a normal approximation poor. A normal model is continuous, so single exact values have probability zero while intervals have positive probability. For this lesson all needed cumulative probabilities are supplied; no outside table is required.

examples.prompt: Assume X is approximately normal with mean 50 and standard deviation 4. Estimate the percentage from 42 to 58 using the 95% rule.
steps: The endpoints are 50−2·4 and 50+2·4.
Thus the interval spans two standard deviations on either side.
The supplied normal rule assigns about 95%; it is a model estimate, not an exact sample count.

examples.prompt: For a standard normal Z, use Φ(1)=0.8413 and Φ(−1)=0.1587 to find P(−1<Z<1).
steps: The cumulative value at 1 includes all probability below that bound.
Subtract the part below −1.
0.8413−0.1587=0.6826, consistent with the approximate 68% rule.

items.answer: The exact-point probability is 0; the interval probability is positive

steps: Random samples fluctuate around model proportions.

weeks.title: Simulation and chance-model checks
weeks.objective: Build chance simulations and interpret unusual outcomes under an explicit model.
days: Define one simulation trial and calibrate random-digit mappings to the stated probabilities.
Work the upper-tail example with ties included and explain its conditional interpretation.
Use worksheet B to define two-sided extremeness before counting outcomes.
Run the supplied digit sequence and evaluate model-check conclusions in worksheet C.
Specify a reproducible simulation plan and explain why zero extreme repetitions does not prove impossibility.
explanation: A simulation imitates a stated chance process with an explicit mechanism. Define one trial, how random values map to outcomes, which statistic is recorded, and how many repetitions are made. A fair-coin model might map random digits 0–4 to heads and 5–9 to tails; equal-sized digit groups encode probability 1/2.

To assess an observed statistic, compare it with statistics from many simulated repetitions under the proposed model. For a preselected upper-tail question, count simulated statistics at least as large as observed, including ties. For a two-sided question, define extremeness on both sides before counting. The tail fraction estimates how unusual the observation would be if the model were correct.

A small simulated tail fraction is evidence against the chance model or its assumptions; it is not the probability the model is true. A large fraction means the observation is not unusual under that model, not that the model is proved. Finite simulations fluctuate, and zero extreme repetitions does not establish zero theoretical probability.

examples.prompt: Under a fair-coin model, 200 simulations of 20 flips produce 9 samples with at least 15 heads. The observed sample has 15 heads. Estimate the upper-tail fraction.
steps: The statistic is the number of heads in a 20-flip sample.
At least 15 includes outcomes equal to the observed count.
Divide the 9 extreme simulations by all 200; this is a model-based tail estimate, not a probability the coin is fair.

examples.prompt: Design a random-digit simulation for success probability 0.3 in five independent trials.
examples.answer: Use digits 0–2 for success, 3–9 for failure; group five independent digits and count successes
steps: Three of ten equally likely digits encode probability 0.3.
Each group of five represents one repeated experiment.
Record the count and repeat many groups, keeping the same statistic and mapping.

worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning, state any domain restrictions, and check your result. Give exact answers unless the item requests rounding. A defensible equivalent explanation is acceptable.

items.prompt: Map equally likely digits 0–9 to an event with probability 0.6.
steps: Six of ten digits must represent success.
Any fixed six-digit subset gives the specified probability.

items.prompt: In 500 simulated samples, 35 statistics are at least the observed value. Find the upper-tail estimate.
steps: Count includes ties as specified.
Divide 35 by 500.

items.prompt: A simulation records 1000 fair-die rolls. What is one trial if studying a single roll?
items.answer: One random integer 1–6, each equally likely
steps: The trial must match one real-model die roll.
Record the selected face or an explicitly defined statistic from it.

items.prompt: Why must simulated flips be independent when the model assumes independent coin flips?
items.answer: Dependence would change the modeled distribution
steps: The probability for each next flip must not be altered by previous simulated outcomes.
A mechanism with forced alternation, for example, is not the independent model.

items.prompt: A tail count is 0 in 100 simulations. Does that prove the event impossible?
steps: Finite runs can miss possible rare outcomes.
More repetitions or theoretical calculation are needed to assess a very small probability.

items.prompt: Observed count is 8; the rule says at least as large. Which simulated counts qualify: 6,8,9,11?

Only 6 lies below the threshold.

worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning, state any domain restrictions, and check your result. Give exact answers unless the item requests rounding. A defensible equivalent explanation is acceptable.

items.prompt: A fair-coin simulation maps digits 0–3 to heads and 4–9 to tails. Is it correctly calibrated?
steps: Four of ten digits map to heads.
A fair model needs five digits for each outcome.

items.prompt: A null-model statistic is centered at 10. Define two-sided extremeness for observed 14 using absolute distance.
steps: Observed distance from the center is 4.
Both equally distant tails count, including the boundary.

items.prompt: Of 800 simulated statistics, 12 are ≤6 and 18 are ≥14. Find that two-sided tail estimate.
steps: The two disjoint tail counts total 30.

items.prompt: Two runs estimate the same tail fraction as 0.048 and 0.053. Must one be wrong?
steps: Simulation estimates have random variation.
Small differences are expected in finite repeated runs.

items.prompt: Explain why 0.04 as a tail fraction is not a 4% probability that the null model is true.
items.answer: It conditions on the model and describes simulated data extremeness
steps: The calculation assumes the model to generate repetitions.
It does not assign probabilities to the competing models themselves.

items.prompt: A proposed process succeeds with probability 1/4. Describe a spinner simulation with four equal sectors.
items.answer: Label one sector success and three failure
steps: Equal sectors make each outcome equally likely.
One successful sector gives probability 1/4 per independent spin.

worksheets.directions: Show the reasoning, state any domain restrictions, and check your result. Give exact answers unless the item requests rounding. A defensible equivalent explanation is acceptable.

items.prompt: An observed mean is 18. A prechosen upper-tail simulation gives 6 of 300 means at least 18. Estimate and interpret.
items.answer: 0.02; the observed mean is uncommon under the simulated model
steps: This provides evidence against that model’s adequacy, with finite-simulation and design limits.

items.prompt: An observation lies near the center of the simulated distribution. Does this prove the model correct?
steps: Many possible models may produce ordinary values there.

items.prompt: Random digits 8,0,5,2,1 are supplied. Using 0–2 as success, count successes in this five-trial sample.
steps: Digits 0,2,1 qualify.

items.prompt: A simulated sample should contain 20 draws with replacement from labels 1–10. Explain what replacement changes.

steps: Return the chosen label before the next draw.
Without replacement the process would have different dependence and cannot even make 20 distinct draws from 10 labels.

items.prompt: A researcher changes an upper-tail rule to a two-sided rule only after seeing the observation. Why should the rule be stated before comparison?
items.answer: Post hoc changes alter what counts as evidence
steps: A predetermined statistic and tail criterion define the chance comparison.
Choosing the rule to suit the observed result can exaggerate apparent evidence.

items.prompt: For 1000 simulations, 62 have statistic≥7 and 21 have statistic≤−7. The null center is 0 and observed value is −7. Find the absolute-distance tail fraction.
steps: Both tails at least 7 from zero count.
(62+21)/1000=0.083; use both signs despite the negative observation.

weeks.title: Sampling distributions and margins of error
weeks.objective: Interpret repeated-sample spread and simulation-based uncertainty.
days: Calculate sample proportions, interval endpoints, signed errors, and percentage-point changes.
Use the worked simulations to distinguish a sampling distribution from individual responses.
Compute empirical coverage and compare sampling precision in worksheet B.
Critique overlap, undercoverage, and mean-interval interpretations in worksheet C.
Explain the long-run meaning of a calibrated interval procedure and separate sampling uncertainty from selection bias.
explanation: A sample proportion p-hat is the fraction of sampled observations with a characteristic. Repeated random samples of the same size from one population will generally produce different estimates. The distribution of those estimates is a sampling distribution, distinct from the distribution of individual observations. Increasing sample size usually reduces sampling spread without repairing selection bias.

A simulation from a specified population can reveal the typical size of estimation errors. If about 95% of simulated estimates lie within 0.06 of the population proportion, 0.06 is an approximate simulation-based 95% error bound for that setup. A report p-hat±0.06 describes an uncertainty interval, not a guarantee that every random sample errs by at most 0.06.

In real inference the population parameter is unknown. Methods calibrated by repeated sampling produce intervals that capture the fixed parameter at their advertised long-run rate under appropriate assumptions. Do not interpret a 95% procedure as saying 95% of individuals fall in the interval, or that an interval cures nonresponse bias. Keep percentage points distinct from percent change and describe simulation limits.

examples.prompt: A random sample has 84 successes among 140 observations. A supplied calibrated error bound is 0.08. Report the estimate and interval.
steps: Divide successes by sample size: 84/140=0.6.
Subtract and add the 0.08 bound.
The interval concerns a population proportion, not a range for individual yes/no observations.

examples.prompt: A known population proportion is 0.40. In 200 simulations, 190 sample proportions lie from 0.34 to 0.46. Describe the observed error coverage.
examples.answer: 95% of these simulations had absolute error at most 0.06
steps: The endpoints differ from the true 0.40 by 0.06.
This is empirical simulation coverage for that setup, not a universal guarantee.

weeks.title: Randomized treatment comparisons
weeks.objective: Compute effects and use shuffled-label simulations under no-effect assumptions.

connection.before: Sample statistics, random assignment, and simulation tails.

days: Compute group means and fix the subtraction order for each treatment comparison.
Build the worked shuffled-label comparison, preserving outcomes and original group sizes.
Count both tails under an absolute-difference criterion in worksheet B.
Use worksheet C to examine missing outcomes, recruitment scope, and practical effect size.
Write a randomized-study conclusion containing effect units, simulation evidence, design assumptions, and a generalization limit.
explanation: A randomized experiment compares a response across treatment groups assigned by chance. A simple statistic is mean(response in A) minus mean(response in B), with the order stated before analysis. Its sign depends on this order and whether a larger response is desirable. An improvement score may control a baseline descriptively, but random assignment is still the basis of the causal comparison.

Under a no-treatment-effect model compatible with random assignment, treatment labels can be shuffled while keeping responses and group sizes fixed. Each shuffle gives a new difference of means. Compare the observed difference with the shuffled distribution using the chosen one-sided or two-sided criterion. The procedure asks how assignment alone could produce differences, not whether any individual was unaffected.

A small tail fraction supports evidence of a treatment difference under the design assumptions. Also report effect size and units: a tiny difference can be statistically unusual in a large study yet unimportant for the decision. Missing outcomes, unequal implementation, or interference between participants can undermine the experiment. Generalization remains limited by recruitment and study conditions.

examples.prompt: Randomized group A has outcomes 8,10,12 and group B has 5,7,9. Find the difference mean A minus mean B.
steps: A has mean 30/3=10.
B has mean 21/3=7.
Subtract in the stated order: 10−7=3; reversing order would reverse the sign.

examples.prompt: A two-sided shuffled-label comparison uses |difference|≥4. Of 1000 shuffles, 18 have difference≥4 and 22 have difference≤−4. Estimate the tail fraction.
steps: Both tails count under the absolute-difference criterion.
The disjoint counts total 40.
40/1000=0.04 is a chance-model estimate, not the probability the treatment has no effect.

steps: A mean is 6 and B mean is 4.
Subtract 4 from 6.

items.prompt: In a treatment-label shuffle, should the response values themselves be changed?
steps: The observed responses remain fixed under the no-effect rearrangement model.
Only labels are reassigned according to the original randomization design.

items.prompt: An experiment assigns 12 subjects to A and 8 to B. What group sizes should each shuffled reassignment preserve?
steps: The simulation must match the allocation design.
Changing group sizes changes the chance distribution.

items.prompt: An observed A−B difference is −2.5 points. Interpret its sign.
items.answer: A’s sample mean is 2.5 points lower than B’s
steps: The subtraction order is A minus B.
A negative result indicates the first group has the smaller mean.

items.prompt: Of 400 shuffles, 20 give differences at least as large as the observed. Find the upper-tail fraction.
steps: Divide the extreme count by the repetition count.

items.prompt: Does random assignment ensure exactly equal pretreatment means in one experiment?
steps: Chance can still create baseline imbalances.
Assignment protects against systematic allocation patterns in the long run, not exact equality every time.
